flashcards.q: What is the observable symptom of data skew in the Spark UI?
flashcards.a: 199 tasks in a stage finish in seconds; 1 task runs for tens of minutes at near-100% CPU. That task's shuffle-read size is an outlier versus the median, confirming data volume, not a slow node.

flashcards.q: Which Spark version made AQE default-enabled, and which shuffles does it re-plan?
flashcards.a: Spark 3.2.0. It re-plans only at shuffle boundaries (materialization points where real stats exist), and only for the DataFrame/SQL API, never RDDs.

flashcards.q: Name AQE's three features and their default config values.
flashcards.a: 1) coalescePartitions (default true) merges small post-shuffle partitions toward advisoryPartitionSizeInBytes (64MB default). 2) automatic join-strategy switch to broadcast if runtime size proves it small enough. 3) skewJoin.enabled (default true): splits a sort-merge join partition exceeding skewedPartitionFactor (5x median) AND skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes (256MB).

flashcards.q: AQE's skew-join handling doesn't fix your skewed job. What two cases does it not cover?
flashcards.a: Aggregation skew (a plain groupBy, not a join) and non-equi joins. Those still require manual salting.

flashcards.q: What is spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold's default, and why is it conservative rather than aggressive?
flashcards.a: 10MB. Conservative because a broadcast materializes the whole 'small' side in the driver then pushes a full copy to every executor; a stale/wrong size estimate under an aggressive threshold risks driver or executor OOM, a worse failure than a slow sort-merge join.

flashcards.q: What causes a BroadcastNestedLoopJoin, and why is it usually a red flag?
flashcards.a: No equality condition available for a hash join (a non-equi join predicate, or an accidental cross join). It's O(n*m) per partition; seeing it unintentionally on two large tables usually means the join condition isn't what was intended.

flashcards.q: What speedup do pandas UDFs give over row-at-a-time Python UDFs, and what mechanism produces it?
flashcards.a: 3x to 100x, because data crosses the JVM/Python boundary in Arrow columnar batches instead of per-row, letting the Python function run vectorized over a pandas Series/DataFrame instead of one row at a time.

flashcards.q: How do newer Arrow UDFs improve on pandas UDFs?
flashcards.a: ~10% faster and ~40% less memory, by operating directly on Arrow's columnar format and skipping the pandas/NumPy materialization step pandas UDFs require.

flashcards.q: Name three concrete cases where .cache() makes a job slower.
flashcards.a: 1) The DataFrame is consumed only once (materialization cost for zero reuse). 2) The cache evicts a more valuable cached DataFrame, forcing its recompute. 3) Caching happens before a filter that would have shrunk the data significantly.

flashcards.q: Describe Spark's Unified Memory Manager layout: what do spark.memory.fraction and spark.memory.storageFraction control?
flashcards.a: memory.fraction (default 0.6) is the share of the executor heap given to the Unified Memory region (execution + storage). storageFraction (default 0.5) is the soft boundary inside that region between storage (cached data) and execution (shuffle/sort/hash-table buffers) — execution can evict storage under pressure, not the reverse.

flashcards.q: What is spark.executor.memoryOverhead's default, and why does it matter especially for PySpark?
flashcards.a: 10% of executor memory, minimum 384MB, off-heap. For PySpark, the separate Python worker process(es) run outside the JVM heap and are effectively budgeted against this overhead — undersizing it starves the Python process while JVM heap graphs look fine.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between spill and OOM?
flashcards.a: Spill is a supported fallback: an operator (sort, aggregate) that exceeds execution memory writes intermediate state to disk and merges later, trading time for staying in bounds. OOM is a hard failure with no such fallback (e.g. broadcast build side, which must be fully in memory by design).

flashcards.q: What does bucketBy do at write time, and when does it fail to pay off?
flashcards.a: Pre-shuffles data into a fixed number of hash buckets by column, so a future join on that same column between two identically-bucketed tables can skip the shuffle. Fails to pay off if the join pattern changes or bucket count/column mismatches between tables — that silently falls back to a full shuffle join, wasting the write-time cost.

flashcards.q: You tripled executor count and the job barely sped up. What should you check before concluding Spark 'doesn't scale' for this workload?
flashcards.a: Check for skew first (one oversized task bottlenecks regardless of idle executors), then serial bottlenecks (driver-side collect, a single broadcast build, few output partitions), then whether the stage is UDF/Python-bound (more executors don't fix per-row Python interpreter overhead).
